themes.name: Sourcing crowds out analysis
themes.insight: The associate and the MD both describe the profile build as data logistics rather than judgment — Alex times it at 70% finding and formatting against 30% analysis and pushes the actual leverage math to the second night — because every input arrives as a filing, a vendor pull, a PDF or a macro feed that has to be re-keyed into one Excel template before any two of them can be compared.

quotes.text: It’s incredibly manual. An associate will spend 48 to 72 hours just building the foundational profile.
quotes.source: P03 — managing director, private credit and liquid strategies, discovery interview

quotes.text: It’s probably 70% finding and formatting, and 30% actual analysis. I feel like a glorified data entry clerk for the first two days.
quotes.source: P01 — investment banking and portfolio associate, discovery interview

quotes.text: That mapping alone easily sucks up 4 to 5 hours of the first day.
quotes.source: P01 — investment banking and portfolio associate, discovery interview

gaps: Only three participants, and all three sit on the same side of one firm's deal chain — an MD, an associate, a credit risk director. Nothing here tests whether the workflow generalizes to another manager, and the Portfolio Operations team named as a secondary user in the brief was not interviewed.

No participant described the predictive deal-sourcing use case. All three talked about building and reviewing a profile for a target already on the desk; the value proposition's claim to identify targets before they launch formal auction processes has no user evidence behind it in this corpus.

Deployment isolation was raised only by Marcus, in one sentence, and no security, compliance or IT stakeholder was interviewed — so the PRD's single-tenant VPC and the RBAC wall between Private Equity and Liquid Strategies are asserted requirements, not validated ones.
No participant gave a volume figure: deals screened per quarter, profiles built per associate, portfolio companies monitored per risk officer. Any reach estimate downstream will be an assumption.

The alternative-data signals in the PRD — employee sentiment indexes, shipping volumes — were named by the product team, not by a participant. Marcus named executive turnover, supply chain delays and accounts payable patterns.

Nobody described what happens after an alert fires: who acts, in which tool, on what timeline, and what an acceptable false-positive rate would be. The 1.5σ threshold and the Credit Health Score are PRD constructs no participant was asked to react to.

Elena described the review of a finished profile and Alex described building one, but no participant walked through the moment of handoff itself, so the rework loop is described from both ends and observed from neither.

The Product Brief, competitive analysis and PRD in the same document are product-team authored. They were read as context and framing; no theme above is grounded in them, and source_count counts only the three interviews.

corpus.method: Three semi-structured discovery interviews, 45–60 minutes each, with practitioners across the full deal lifecycle — origination, credit review and post-close monitoring.
known_bias: Three participants is enough to find the shape of a workflow and not enough to size anything. Every frequency in this synthesis is out of three.
All three work at mid-market private credit desks. Nothing here speaks to large-cap syndicated processes or to desks with an existing data vendor.

Each participant was interviewed once, in one sitting. This records what they say they do; it does not record what they actually do, and self-reported time estimates skew high for tasks people resent.
All three were referred by the same two desks, so a shared house method may read as an industry norm.
